description: Union-find (disjoint set) decomposed. Two operations: find (which group is x in?) and union (merge two groups). With path compression + union by rank, amortised O(α(n)) per operation — essentially constant. Used in Kruskal's MST, dynamic connectivity, image processing, equivalence relations.

sub_mechanisms.name: parent_array_representation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each element has a parent pointer. parent[x] = x means x is its own root (group representative).
sub_mechanisms.why: Trees encode group membership. Each tree represents one group. Root identifies the group. Forest of disjoint trees = the disjoint sets.

sub_mechanisms.name: find_operation
sub_mechanisms.definition: find(x): follow parent pointers from x until reaching a root (parent[r] == r). Return r.
sub_mechanisms.why: Root identifies the group. Two elements are in the same group iff they have the same root. Naive find is O(depth); with optimisations, ~O(1) amortised.

sub_mechanisms.name: union_operation
sub_mechanisms.definition: union(x, y): find roots rx + ry. If different, set one as parent of the other.
sub_mechanisms.why: Merging groups = pointing one root at the other. Now both trees share a root → same group. Choice of which root becomes parent matters for balance (see union by rank).

sub_mechanisms.name: path_compression
sub_mechanisms.definition: During find, set every traversed node's parent directly to the root. Future finds from those nodes are O(1).
sub_mechanisms.why: Trees get flatter with use. Amortised O(α(n)) per operation when combined with union by rank. Implementation: 1-line addition to find (set parent[x] = root after finding it).

sub_mechanisms.name: union_by_rank
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each root has a rank (upper bound on its tree's height). Union: make the lower-rank root point to the higher-rank one. Equal ranks: pick one, increment its rank.
sub_mechanisms.why: Prevents trees from becoming linear. Combined with path compression, gives amortised O(α(n)). Rank is upper bound, not exact (path compression makes trees shorter than rank suggests).

sub_mechanisms.name: union_by_size
sub_mechanisms.definition: Track tree size. Union: smaller tree's root points to larger's. Functionally equivalent to union by rank.
sub_mechanisms.why: Simpler conceptually + provides additional info (size of each component). Same asymptotic behaviour as union by rank. Common in implementations that need component sizes anyway.

sub_mechanisms.name: amortised_inverse_ackermann
sub_mechanisms.definition: With path compression + union by rank/size, m operations on n elements take O(m · α(n)) time. α is the inverse Ackermann function.
sub_mechanisms.why: Tarjan's classical analysis. α(n) ≤ 4 for n ≤ 2^65536 (essentially all possible inputs). Effectively constant per operation, though not strictly O(1). One of the most beautiful results in algorithm analysis.

sub_mechanisms.name: Kruskal_use_case
sub_mechanisms.definition: Kruskal's MST: sort edges by weight; for each edge, if endpoints in different components (find), add to MST + union.
sub_mechanisms.why: Union-find is what makes Kruskal's O(E log E). Cycle detection becomes O(α(n)) per edge instead of O(V) graph search. The clean separation between sort + connectivity-tracking is what makes Kruskal's elegant.

sub_mechanisms.name: incremental_connectivity
sub_mechanisms.definition: Dynamic connectivity in graphs being built: each edge addition is a union; queries are find-then-compare.
sub_mechanisms.why: Online problem (edges arrive over time). Union-find handles each edge in O(α(n)). For fully dynamic (edges added + removed), more complex structures (Euler-tour tree) needed.

sub_mechanisms.name: weighted_union_find
sub_mechanisms.definition: Variant: each edge has a weight; track weight differences between elements + their roots. find returns root + weight diff.
sub_mechanisms.why: Equivalence classes with relative weights. Used in solving systems of equations where variables are related by additive constants (a - b = c). Same O(α(n)) per operation.

derivation_rules.name: path_compression_and_union_by_rank_give_inverse_ackermann
then: amortised cost is O(α(n)) per operation
derivation_rules.why: Tarjan's proof (1975). Without either, operations degrade: O(log n) with one, O(n) with neither. The combination is what gives the near-constant bound. Implementing both is essentially free (a few lines).

derivation_rules.name: find_idempotent_after_compression
if: path compression has run on x's lineage
derivation_rules.why: Compression sets parent[x] = root. Next find(x) returns immediately. Compression's benefit accumulates: warm-up phase has cost; subsequent finds are essentially free.

derivation_rules.name: Kruskal_O_E_log_E_via_union_find
if: Kruskal uses union-find for cycle detection
then: total runtime is O(E log E)
derivation_rules.why: Sort: O(E log E). For each edge: find × 2 + union = O(α(n)). Total: O(E log E + E · α(n)) = O(E log E). Without union-find, cycle detection per edge would be O(V) (DFS/BFS), giving O(E · V) — much slower.

derivation_rules.name: union_by_size_or_rank_keeps_tree_shallow
if: smaller tree is attached to larger
derivation_rules.why: Each time a tree's depth grows, it merges with one of at least equal size — doubling its size. After k depth increases, tree has at least 2^k elements. So depth ≤ log n. Path compression makes this even better.

derivation_rules.name: α_n_essentially_constant_for_practical_n
derivation_rules.why: Ackermann's function grows astronomically fast; its inverse grows astronomically slow. For any input we could ever process, α(n) is bounded by a small constant. Practically equivalent to O(1) per operation.
